questions.title: Cracking a bank
questions.text: Crackers broke into the online banking system of a bank in Kazakhstan. They used a phishing e-mail to steal an employee's password, then copied the personal details of 20 000 customers.

scheme.mark_scheme: - gaining unauthorised access to a computer system / data (with malicious intent) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Cracking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system or data, usually to cause harm or for gain.

parts.title: Phishing
parts.text: Describe how a phishing e-mail could be used to steal the employee's password.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- fake e-mail that looks genuine / from the bank or IT department (1)
- link to a fake website / form where the employee enters the password, which is sent to the cracker (1)
scheme.model_answer: The cracker sends an e-mail that looks as if it came from the bank's IT department with a link to a fake log-in page; when the employee types their password, it is sent to the cracker.

parts.title: Ethical problems
parts.text: Analyse **two** ethical problems arising from this attack.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two problems, each with analysis (1 + 1):
- customers' privacy violated (1) → details may be sold / used for identity theft or fraud (1)
- loss of trust in the bank / online banking (1) → customers stop using e-services / move bank (1)
- innocent people harmed (1) → stress, financial loss (1)
scheme.model_answer: Customers' privacy has been violated: their personal details may be sold and used for identity theft, so innocent people can lose money. Customers also lose trust in the bank and in online banking generally, so they may stop using e-services.

parts.title: Legal consequence
parts.text: State **one** legal consequence for the crackers if they are caught.

scheme.mark_scheme: - fine / correctional work / imprisonment under the Criminal Code (1)
scheme.model_answer: They can be imprisoned under the Criminal Code of Kazakhstan for unauthorised access.

questions.title: Protecting the bank's systems
questions.text: After the attack, the bank's IT manager wants to protect the customer database from unauthorised access.

parts.title: Two-factor authentication
parts.text: Explain how **two-factor authentication** would have stopped the attack in question 1.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- a second factor (code on phone / fingerprint / token) is needed besides the password (1)
- the cracker had only the stolen password, so could not log in (1)
scheme.model_answer: Staff would need a one-time code from their phone as well as their password; the cracker had only the stolen password, so could not log in.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- authentication checks who the user is (password, biometrics) (1)
- authorisation decides what the user may access / do (access rights) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Authentication checks who the user is, for example by password and fingerprint; authorisation decides what that user may do, such as read-only access to customer records.

parts.title: Two more measures
parts.text: Describe **two** other measures the bank can use to protect the customer data from unauthorised access.

scheme.mark_scheme: Two measures, each identified (1) and described (1): encryption — stolen data cannot be read without key; hashing passwords — stolen password file does not reveal passwords; limited access rights — staff see only what they need; limiting login attempts — stops brute force; firewall — blocks unauthorised connections; logs / audit trails — detect misuse; blocking unknown locations; updates / patches; staff training against phishing
scheme.model_answer: Encrypt the customer database, so that even if it is copied the data cannot be read without the key. Give staff limited access rights, so that each employee can see only the records needed for their job and one stolen account exposes less data.

questions.title: Malware in a school
questions.text: A school network of 300 computers becomes very slow. The technician finds that a worm has copied itself to almost every computer. Two weeks later a teacher installs a "free mark calculator" that turns out to be a Trojan horse.

parts.title: Worm vs virus
parts.text: Explain why the malware that spread to almost every computer is a **worm** and not a virus.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- a worm spreads by itself across the network / self-replicates (1)
- a virus needs a host file and a user to run / share it (1)
scheme.model_answer: A worm copies itself across the network without any user action, while a virus needs a host file that a user runs or shares; copies reached almost every computer by themselves.

parts.title: Trojan
parts.text: Describe how the Trojan horse got onto the teacher's computer and **one** problem it could cause.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- disguised as useful software, installed by the teacher (1)
- opens a back door / steals data such as marks or passwords (1)
scheme.model_answer: It pretended to be a useful mark calculator, so the teacher installed it; it can open a back door so a cracker can steal pupils' personal data.

parts.title: Problems for the school
parts.text: Analyse **one** problem the malware causes for the school.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- problem: slow / unusable network / downtime, or data stolen (1)
- consequence: lessons and online tests cannot run / pupils' data leaked → privacy breach, fines (1)
scheme.model_answer: The worm uses the network's bandwidth so computers are very slow, which means lessons and online tests cannot run and teaching time is lost.

parts.title: Countermeasures
parts.text: State **two** measures the school should take to prevent malware infections.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): up-to-date anti-malware; firewall; install patches / updates; only install software from trusted sources / admin rights needed to install; do not open unknown attachments; staff training; regular offline backups
scheme.model_answer: Install anti-malware software with updated signatures, and allow only the administrator to install new software.

questions.title: Ransomware in a clinic
questions.text: A private clinic in Almaty is hit by ransomware. All patient records are encrypted and the criminals demand payment within 48 hours.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- malware that encrypts the victim's files (1)
- and demands a payment / ransom for the key (1)
scheme.model_answer: Ransomware is malware that encrypts the victim's files so they cannot be opened and demands a ransom for the decryption key.

parts.title: Problems for patients and clinic
parts.text: Analyse the problems this attack causes for the **clinic** and for its **patients**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Clinic (max 2): downtime — appointments cancelled / no access to records (1) → loss of income / reputation / fines / recovery costs (1)
Patients (max 2): treatment delayed (1) → health risk; data may be leaked (1) → privacy / blackmail
scheme.model_answer: The clinic cannot open records, so appointments are cancelled and it loses income and reputation. Patients' treatment is delayed, which is a risk to their health, and their medical data may be published, which violates their privacy.

parts.title: Pay or not?
parts.text: Explain why paying the ransom is **not** recommended.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): no guarantee the key is given / files restored; funds criminals / encourages more attacks; the clinic may be targeted again; data may still be leaked
scheme.model_answer: There is no guarantee the criminals will send the key, and paying funds criminals and encourages further attacks on the clinic and others.

questions.title: A privacy policy
questions.text:
A new food-delivery app in Kazakhstan asks users to accept its privacy policy. Part of it says:

*"We collect your name, phone number and location to deliver your orders. We share your phone number with the courier. Order history is kept for 3 years. You may ask us to correct or delete your data."*

parts.title: Purpose of a privacy policy
parts.text: Explain the purpose of a privacy policy.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- tells users what personal data is collected and how it is used / stored / shared (1)
- so users can give informed consent / know their rights / legal requirement / accountability (1)
scheme.model_answer: It tells users what personal data is collected and how it is used, stored and shared, so that they can give informed consent and know their rights.

parts.title: Read the policy
parts.text: Complete the table using the extract from the policy.

prefill: Purpose of collecting the data
Who the data is shared with
How long order history is kept

scheme.mark_scheme: Purpose: to deliver orders (1); Shared with: the courier (1); Storage period: 3 years (1)
scheme.model_answer: Purpose — to deliver orders; Shared with — the courier; Storage period — 3 years.

parts.title: Missing item
parts.text: State **one** other item that the full privacy policy should contain.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): how data is protected / security; cookies; contact details; how users are told about changes; rules for children; where data is stored; right to withdraw consent
scheme.model_answer: How the data is protected, for example by encryption.

parts.title: Problem with policies
parts.text: Explain **one** problem with relying on privacy policies to protect users.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- policies are long / legal language so users do not read them (1) → users agree without knowing how data is used (1)
OR must accept to use the service (1) → no real choice (1)
OR a policy does not guarantee security (1) → data can still be leaked (1)
scheme.model_answer: Policies are long and written in legal language, so most users accept them without reading and do not really know how their data will be used.

summary: The ethical and legal problems caused by cracking (hacking) computer systems, how to protect data from unauthorised access (authentication, authorisation, encryption, hashing and more), the problems caused by different types of malware, and what privacy policies are, what they contain and why they matter.

blocks.content: **Gaining unauthorised access** to a computer system, network or data — by guessing or stealing passwords, exploiting software weaknesses or tricking people. **Cracking** usually means breaking into systems or breaking software protection **with malicious intent**.
Using a computer system, account or data **without the permission of its owner** — even if nothing is changed, copied or damaged.
A **weakness** in software, hardware, a network or a procedure (for example an unpatched bug or a weak password) that an attacker can **exploit** to get in.

items.title: Black-hat hackers (crackers)
items.content: Break into systems **illegally** for personal gain or to cause harm: stealing money or data, blackmail, sabotage.

items.title: White-hat (ethical) hackers
items.content: Security experts who test systems **with the owner's permission** (penetration testing) to find weaknesses and fix them before criminals exploit them.

items.title: Grey-hat hackers
items.content: Break in **without permission** but without criminal intent — e.g. to report a weakness. Still **illegal** and ethically questionable.

blocks.title: Common cracking methods
rows: A program tries **every possible password** until one works
Long, complex passwords; limit login attempts
Tries common words and leaked passwords
Passwords that are not words or names; 2FA
Tricks people into **revealing passwords** with fake e-mails, websites or phone calls
User training; 2FA; check the address of links
Uses **bugs in unpatched software** to get in
Types SQL code into a web form to read or change the database
Captures data sent over an **unencrypted** network, e.g. public Wi-Fi
Records the keys a user types, including passwords

blocks.caption: How crackers get in — and the layer that stops each attack

blocks.title: SQL injection in a school login form
blocks.content:
A login page builds this query from what the user types:
`SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = '` + *name* + `' AND Password = '` + *password* + `'`

A cracker types `' OR '1'='1` as the password. The query becomes `… AND Password = '' OR '1'='1'` — the condition is **always true**, so the cracker is logged in without a password.
**Protection:** validate input and use **parameterised queries**, so typed text is treated as data, never as SQL code.

theory.title: Ethical and legal problems of cracking

blocks.content: The **moral principles** that decide whether an action is right or wrong. An action can be legal but unethical, or (as with most cracking) both **illegal and unethical**.

blocks.title: Problems caused by cracking
rows: **Identity theft** — criminals use stolen personal details
**Financial loss** — stolen money, fines, cost of recovery
Loss of **trust** in online banking, e-government, shopping
Theft of money from bank accounts
**Theft of confidential data** — customers' details, trade secrets
**Invasion of privacy** — private messages, photos published
Cost passed to everyone through higher prices and taxes

blocks.title: Ethical problems and legal problems
rows: Society's values, professional codes of conduct
Courts, under laws such as the Criminal Code
Violating privacy, harming innocent people, breaking trust, using leaked data
Unauthorised access, data theft, fraud, failing to protect personal data
Loss of trust and reputation, harm to people

items.title: Why cracking is unethical
items.content:
- It **violates privacy** — people have a right to control their personal data.
- It is **theft** of property (data, money, intellectual property) even if nothing physical is taken.
- It **harms innocent people** — customers, patients, employees.
- It **breaks trust** between people and organisations.
- "I only looked, I did not change anything" is still **unauthorised access**.

items.title: Legal consequences
items.content:
- In Kazakhstan, unauthorised access to computer information is a crime under the **Criminal Code** (fines, correctional work, imprisonment).
- Organisations that fail to protect personal data can be fined under the **Law on Personal Data and its Protection**.
- Most countries have similar laws (e.g. the UK **Computer Misuse Act**, the EU **GDPR**).

blocks.title: Ethical dilemma — analyse it
blocks.content:
*A student discovers that the school's marking website lets anyone see every pupil's marks by changing a number in the address bar. She shows her friends.*

- **Ethical problem:** she accessed other pupils' **private data** without permission and shared it — a breach of their privacy.
- **Legal problem:** this is **unauthorised access**, even though the website was badly designed.
- **The right action:** report the weakness **privately** to the school's IT staff (responsible disclosure) without using or sharing the data.
- **The school's responsibility:** it failed to protect personal data and must fix the vulnerability.
Use a chain: **what happened → who is harmed → how they are harmed → why it is wrong (privacy, theft, trust)**. One mark is usually for the problem and one for its consequence.
Checking **who a user is** before giving access — with something the user **knows** (password, PIN), **has** (phone, smart card) or **is** (fingerprint, face).
Deciding **what an authenticated user is allowed to do** — which files or records they can read, change or delete.
Scrambling data with an algorithm and a **key** so that it can only be read by someone with the correct key. Stolen or intercepted encrypted data is **unreadable**.

blocks.title: Measures against unauthorised access
rows: Long passwords with upper and lower case, digits and symbols are much harder to guess or brute-force
A stolen password is not enough — a second factor (phone code, fingerprint) is needed
The account is locked after several wrong passwords → stops brute-force attacks
Each user can only read or change the data needed for their job (**principle of least privilege**)
Stolen or intercepted data cannot be read; **SSL/TLS (HTTPS)** protects data in transit
The database stores only a hash, so stolen password files do not reveal the passwords
Close the vulnerabilities that crackers exploit
Record who accessed what and when, so misuse is detected
**Blocking access from certain locations / IP addresses**
Only allows log-in from trusted networks or countries
Staff recognise phishing and do not share passwords
Locked server rooms, screen locks when staff leave their desks

blocks.title: Authentication vs authorisation
rows: Access rights: read, write, delete, execute
A teacher logs in with a password and code
The teacher can edit marks, a pupil can only view their own

blocks.title: Encryption vs hashing
rows: **Two-way** — can be decrypted with the key
Data that must be read again: files, messages, data in transit (HTTPS)
Attacker gets hashes, not the passwords

blocks.title: How to protect a school database against cracking
items: **Authenticate** every user: strong passwords plus **two-factor authentication** for staff.
**Limit login attempts** and lock accounts after repeated failures.
**Authorise** carefully: pupils read only their own marks, teachers edit only their classes (least privilege).
**Encrypt** data in transit (HTTPS / SSL-TLS) and stored data; **hash** passwords.
Keep software **updated**, use a **firewall**, and keep **logs** of who accessed what.
**Train** staff to recognise phishing.

blocks.content:
- Mixing up **authentication** (who you are) and **authorisation** (what you can do).
- Saying encryption **stops** data being stolen — it stops stolen data being **read**.
- Writing "use a password" — exam answers need the **feature** (complexity, 2FA, lockout) and **how it helps**.
- Saying a firewall removes viruses — a firewall **filters network traffic**.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Define the term cracking. [1]**
Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system or data, usually with malicious intent / to cause harm or for gain (1).

**Q: The school database is always at risk of system cracking. Describe two ways to protect it. [4]**
Two-factor authentication (1): a code from the user's phone is needed as well as the password, so a stolen password alone does not give access (1). Limit login attempts (1): the account is locked after a few wrong passwords, which stops brute-force attacks (1). *(Also: complex passwords, SSL/TLS, encryption, hashing, access rights.)*

**Q: Give two measures that a company can take to protect confidential data from being stolen. [2]**
Encrypting data (1); granting limited access rights (1). *(Also: blocking access from certain locations, keeping logs of user entries.)*

**Q: Analyse one ethical problem that arises when a hacker cracks a hospital system. [2]**
Patients' confidential medical records may be exposed or sold, violating their privacy (1), which can lead to discrimination or blackmail / treatment may be delayed, putting lives at risk (1).

**Q: Explain the difference between authentication and authorisation. [2]**
Authentication checks who the user is, e.g. password or fingerprint (1); authorisation decides what that user may access or do, e.g. read-only rights (1).

- Listing measures without saying **how** each one protects the data (the second mark).
- Giving a consequence that is not **ethical** when asked for an ethical problem — talk about privacy, harm, trust.
- Writing "hackers are bad" — name the **type** of hacker and what makes the action illegal (no permission).

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: Define cracking, unauthorised access and vulnerability.
Compare black-hat, white-hat and grey-hat hackers.
Name five cracking methods and a countermeasure for each.
Analyse one ethical and one legal problem caused by cracking a hospital or bank.
Explain authentication vs authorisation, and encryption vs hashing.
Describe how 2FA and limiting login attempts protect an account.

blocks.content: Software designed to **damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access** to a computer system or data.
The **harmful action** that malware carries out once it is on a computer — deleting files, encrypting data, stealing passwords, opening a back door.

blocks.title: Types of malware and their effects
rows: Attaches to a program or file; spreads when the infected file is run or shared
Corrupts or deletes files, slows the computer
**Spreads by itself** across networks, without user action
Uses bandwidth, slows or crashes networks, carries other malware
Disguised as **useful software**; the user installs it
Opens a **back door** for crackers, steals data
Demands **payment** for the key; data loss, downtime
Annoying, slows the computer, may lead to dangerous sites
Lets a criminal control many infected computers
Hides other malware, gives full control to the attacker

items.title: Problems for individuals
items.content:
- **Loss of data** (photos, documents) and money (ransom, stolen bank details).
- **Identity theft** and invasion of privacy.
- Slow or unusable computer; cost of repair.

items.title: Problems for organisations and society
items.content:
- **Downtime** — hospitals, airlines or factories stop working (e.g. the WannaCry ransomware attack on hospitals in 2017).
- **Financial loss** — ransom, recovery, lost business, fines for leaked data.
- **Reputation damage** and loss of customer trust.
- Attacks on **critical infrastructure**; spread of spam and fake news through botnets.

blocks.caption: A ransomware attack on a clinic — and the way out

blocks.title: Analysing a malware problem — a clinic
blocks.content:
*A clinic's receptionist opens an e-mail attachment. Overnight, ransomware encrypts every patient record and demands payment.*
- **Problem for the clinic:** **downtime** — appointments cancelled, staff cannot see medical histories; cost of recovery and possible **fines** if data leaked.
- **Problem for patients:** treatment **delayed**; their personal data may be **published** if the ransom is not paid (privacy).
- **Ethical problem:** paying the ransom **funds criminals** and encourages further attacks, but not paying may harm patients.
- **Prevention:** staff training on phishing, anti-malware with updated signatures, patches, limited user rights, **regular offline backups**.

blocks.title: Countermeasures
blocks.content: Anti-virus software with up-to-date signatures, firewalls, software updates, not opening unknown attachments or links, downloading only from trusted sources, limited user rights and **regular offline backups** (see **Data protection measures**).

- Confusing a **virus** (needs a host file and user action) with a **worm** (spreads on its own).
- Calling every piece of malware a "virus" — name the **type** that fits the scenario.
- Saying **anti-virus** blocks hackers or a **firewall** removes viruses.
- Listing problems without saying **who** is affected and **how**.

A **legal document** published by an organisation (on its website or app) that **explains what personal data it collects, why it collects it, how it is used, stored and protected, who it is shared with, and what rights the user has**.
Any information that **identifies a living person**, directly or indirectly — name, IIN, phone, address, photo, location, IP address.
The user's **clear agreement** to the collection and use of their personal data for a stated purpose. It should be **informed** (the user knows what they agree to) and can be **withdrawn**.

blocks.title: What a privacy policy contains
rows: Which personal data is collected: name, e-mail, phone, location, IP address, cookies, payment details
**Why** the data is collected: providing the service, processing orders, improving the website, advertising
Whether data is **shared with or sold to third parties** (advertisers, partners, government)
**How long** data is kept, **where** it is stored (country), how it is **protected** (encryption)
Which cookies are used and how to switch them off
The right to **access, correct, delete** the data, to withdraw **consent**, to complain
Special rules for users under a certain age
Who to contact about data, and how users are told about changes to the policy

items.title: Why privacy policies are needed
items.content:
- **Laws require them** — e.g. the Kazakhstan Law on Personal Data and its Protection, the EU GDPR.
- Users can make an **informed decision** before giving their data (**consent**).
- They make organisations **accountable** for how they use data.
- They build **trust** between users and the organisation.

items.title: Problems with privacy policies
items.content:
- Often **very long and written in legal language**, so most people do not read them.
- Users must often accept them to use the service ("take it or leave it").
- Policies can **change**, and data already given may be used in new ways.
- A policy does not guarantee the data is actually secure.

blocks.title: Reading a privacy policy (exam style)
blocks.content:
An app's policy says: *"We collect your location to show nearby shops. We share anonymised location data with advertising partners. Data is kept for 12 months. You can delete your account at any time."*
- **Data collected:** location.
- **Purpose:** to show nearby shops.
- **Sharing:** anonymised data given to advertisers.
- **Storage period:** 12 months.
- **User right:** to delete the account.

blocks.title: How to evaluate a privacy policy before you sign up
items: Find **what data** is collected — is it more than the service needs?
Find the **purpose** — is every item of data really needed for it?
Check **sharing** — is data sold to advertisers or sent abroad?
Check **storage** — how long, where, and is it encrypted?
Check your **rights** — can you see, correct and delete your data and withdraw consent?

blocks.content:
- Describing a privacy policy as "a policy about privacy" — say **what it contains**.
- Thinking a privacy policy **protects** data by itself — it **explains** how data is handled; security measures protect it.
- Forgetting **user rights** and **sharing with third parties** — the two items examiners look for most.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Explain the difference between a virus and a worm. [2]**
A virus attaches to a host file and spreads only when the user runs or shares the file (1); a worm is standalone and copies itself across a network without any user action (1).

**Q: A company's computers are infected with ransomware. Analyse two problems this causes for the company. [4]**
Files are encrypted so staff cannot work / downtime (1), so orders are lost and customers go elsewhere (1). The company may pay a ransom or recovery costs (1), and if customer data is leaked it may be fined and lose its reputation (1).

**Q: Describe how a Trojan horse gets onto a computer. [2]**
It is disguised as useful / legitimate software (1), so the user downloads and installs it themselves (1).

**Q: Explain the purpose of a privacy policy. [2]**
It tells users what personal data is collected and how it is used, stored and shared (1), so that they can give informed consent and know their rights (1).

**Q: State three items of information that a privacy policy should contain. [3]**
Any three: data collected; purpose; sharing with third parties; how long it is stored; how it is protected; cookies; user rights; contact details.

- Saying a **firewall** removes viruses, or that **anti-virus** blocks hackers — say what each one actually does.
- Confusing a **virus** (needs a host file and user action) with a **worm** (spreads on its own).
- Describing a privacy policy as "a policy about privacy" — say **what it contains**.
- Giving consequences without **analysing** them: *who* is harmed and *how*.

items: Define malware and payload.
Describe virus, worm, Trojan, spyware, ransomware, adware, botnet and rootkit, and the problems each causes.
Analyse the problems a ransomware attack causes for a hospital and its patients.
Give five countermeasures against malware.
Define privacy policy, personal data and consent.
List six things a privacy policy should explain, and two problems with privacy policies.
